objective: By the end of this lesson you can pick the right approach category and circling minimums, stay inside the circling protected area while you maneuver visually to a base or downwind, and fly the correct climbing turn to the missed approach if you lose sight of the airport.
why: Circling is flown low, slow and often at night or in poor visibility, with only your eyes to keep you off the obstacles. Knowing the protected area, the category rules and the missed approach from the circle keeps a routine landing from turning into a stall, spin or CFIT accident.

prereading.what: Aircraft approach categories, the circling approach area and radii, the 2012 expanded circling criteria, and why circling-only procedures exist.
prereading.label: IPH 4-8 to 4-11

prereading.what: Approach category definition and limits, using higher category minimums when faster, and how bank, speed, wind and technique change your ground track.
prereading.label: AIM 5-4-7, 5-4-30 to 5-4-31

prereading.what: Circling protected areas (standard and expanded radii, the C symbol), circling minimums and restrictions, and the missed approach while circling.
prereading.label: AIM 5-4-20 to 5-4-21, 5-4-55 to 5-4-60

prereading.what: A sample approach chart with circling minimums, the four circling patterns, IAP minimums and missed approaches.
prereading.label: IFH 10-19 to 10-21

prereading.what: Autopilot and altitude preselector use, stabilized approach and descent rates, the transition to visual, night circling notes and missed approach.
prereading.label: IPH 4-36 to 4-41

warmup: You break out at the MDA at night with the runway you need on the far side of the airport. What would make you lose sight of it, and which way would you turn if you did?

key_terms.def: A visual maneuver after an instrument approach to line up with a runway when a straight-in landing is not possible or not wanted.
A grouping (A to E) by VREF, or 1.3 VSO if no VREF, at maximum certificated landing weight.
The protected area made of arcs drawn from each runway end and joined by straight tangent lines.
Built before late 2012 with one fixed radius per category. No C symbol on the circling line.
Built after late 2012. Radius grows with category and MDA altitude. Marked with a white C in a black square.
The lowest altitude (MSL) for the circle. Gives at least 300 ft of obstacle clearance inside the circling area.
How high the circling MDA is above the airport elevation.
An approach with no straight-in minimums, named with a letter, such as VOR-A.
A chart note that bans circling in part of the area, for example Circling NA E of Rwy 17-35.
Where the missed approach starts. Circling and straight-in nonprecision lines share the same MAP.

chunks.title: What a circling approach is and when you fly one

body.p: A circling approach is a maneuver you start to line up with a runway when a straight-in landing from an instrument approach is not possible or not wanted [[23:349|IFH G-4]]. The minimums under CIRCLING apply when you need to circle the airport, maneuver for landing, or when no straight-in minimums are published [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].
Some approaches only have circling minimums. They are named with a letter instead of a runway, such as VOR A [[33:398|AIM 5-4-5]]. They are usually built that way because:

bullets: The final approach course is more than 30° off the runway centerline [[29:151|IPH 4-11]].
The descent from the FAF to the threshold crossing height would be steeper than 400 ft per NM [[29:151|IPH 4-11]].
A runway is not clearly defined on the airfield [[29:151|IPH 4-11]].

body.p: ATC may clear you for one approach and a landing on another runway, for example: cleared for VOR Runway 17 approach, circle to land Runway 23 [[29:134|IPH 3-22]]. If the clearance names no landing runway, you may land on any runway [[29:136|IPH 3-24]].

Only circling minimums on the chart does not force you to circle. If you have the active runway in sight in time for a normal approach and ATC has cleared you to land on it, you may land straight in. If you want to circle, tell ATC [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]].

callout.text: Circling is prohibited from a GLS, from an ILS that has no localizer line of minima, and from an RNAV (GPS) approach that has no LNAV line of minima [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].

check.q: A VOR final approach course is 45° off the only runway. What kind of minimums will the chart show?
check.a: Circling minimums only. Straight-in minimums are not published when the course is more than 30° off the runway [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]] [[29:151|IPH 4-11]].

body.p: Your approach category comes from VREF, or from 1.3 VSO if no VREF is given, at the maximum certificated landing weight. These are the values set by the certification authority [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].

head: Category
Speed (VREF or 1.3 VSO)
rows: 91 knots or more but less than 121 knots [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]
121 knots or more but less than 141 knots [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]
141 knots or more but less than 166 knots [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]

body.p: The certified category is permanent. You may never fly to the minimums of a slower category than your airplane's [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. The IPH notes the category speeds are indicated airspeeds [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

callout.text: Flying faster than the top of your category's speed range? Use the minimums for the higher category. AIM examples: a Category B airplane circling at 145 knots uses Category D minimums; a Category A airplane flying a straight-in at 130 knots uses Category C [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]].

body.p: Higher speeds come from gusty wind, icing or non-normal conditions [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]], and from overweight emergency returns or inoperative flaps [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. Work out your approach speed and its category in preflight planning, and review it before the approach [[29:149|IPH 4-9]].

Example math: no VREF is published and VSO is 60 knots. 1.3 × 60 = 78 knots, so the airplane is Category A. If you plan to circle at 95 knots, you are past the 91-knot top of Category A, so use the Category B minimums [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]] [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]].

check.q: Why does flying faster than your category matter on a circling approach?
check.a: A faster airplane makes bigger turns, and the circling area is sized for the category speed. Higher category minimums give a larger protected area [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]] [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

chunks.title: Circling minimums: MDA, HAA and visibility

body.p: Circling minimums are the MDA and the visibility required for the circle-to-land maneuver. The MDA is in feet MSL. The number next to it is the height above airport (HAA) [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]]. When there is no dividing line between categories, one set of minimums covers two or more categories [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].

head: Troy ILS or LOC RWY 7, CIRCLING
MDA-visibility
HAA

body.p: Check: airport elevation is 398 ft, so 940 - 398 = 542 ft HAA [[23:310|IFH 10-19]]. Read the notes too. On this chart, if the local altimeter setting is not received, all MDAs go up 120 ft and circling visibility for Categories C and D goes up ¼ mile [[23:310|IFH 10-19]].

bullets: The circling MDA gives at least 300 ft of obstacle clearance inside the circling area [[23:311|IFH 10-20]] [[33:412|AIM 5-4-5g]].
On an RNAV (GPS) chart, circling minimums can be lower than LNAV/VNAV but never lower than the LNAV straight-in line [[33:411|AIM 5-4-5f]].
Your authorized MDA is the highest of: the procedure's MDA, the MDA set for the pilot in command, and the MDA for the equipment you have and use [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]].
Numbers in parentheses in the minimums, like (600-1), are for military use and are not used in civil aviation [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].

callout.text: Below the MDA only when: you are continuously in a position to descend to the intended runway at a normal rate with normal maneuvers, flight visibility is at least the published visibility, and a required runway reference is distinctly visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]. You may not land if flight visibility is below the published visibility [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]].

check.q: Troy's local altimeter setting is not available. What is the Category C circling MDA and visibility?
check.a: 940 + 120 = 1,060 ft MSL, and 1½ + ¼ = 1¾ SM, per the chart note [[23:310|IFH 10-19]].

chunks.title: The circling protected area: standard and expanded

body.p: The circling area is drawn with arcs from each runway end, joined by straight tangent lines. The radius depends on your approach category [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]]. Obstacle clearance at the MDA only exists while you stay inside this area [[23:42|IFH 1-23]].
There are two kinds of circling area. Look for the white C in a black square on the circling line of minima [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]].

head: Standard (no C symbol)
Expanded (C symbol)
rows: Category and circling MDA altitude, to account for higher TAS up high [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]]
Cat A / B / C / D / E

body.p: The bigger expanded areas give real room to maneuver. The IPH example: at a sea level airport with a 1,500 ft HAA, the Category C radius is 2.86 NM, 1.16 NM (68.5%) larger than before, so pilots don't need high descent rates [[29:149|IPH 4-9]].
Four things change where you actually fly [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7c]] [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c]]:

bullets: Bank angle. At 165 knots groundspeed the turn radius grows from 4,194 ft at 30° bank to 6,654 ft at 20° bank [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7c]].
Indicated airspeed. Design uses the highest speed of the category [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c]].
Wind. On downwind your groundspeed can be much higher than your indicated airspeed, so plan every turn [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c]].
Technique. Plan the lateral and vertical path with the current weather and terrain [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c]].

callout.text: The protection is only at or above the MDA and inside the area. Once below the MDA, you must see and avoid obstacles yourself [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]].

check.q: The circling line shows the C symbol, you are Category B and the circling MDA is 1,840 ft MSL. How far from the runway ends are you protected?
check.a: 1.8 NM. That MDA is in the 1,001 to 3,000 ft row of the expanded table [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]].

body.p: Part of the circling area may be closed by a chart note, written as a direction from a runway. No circling is allowed in that part. A restriction may apply only to some categories, and it can differ between day and night. Review and follow it on every circle [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].

In this example the note reads: Circling not authorized west of Rwy 16-34. Night circling not authorized [[29:226|IPH 4-86]]. Look also at the visibility: Category A needs 1 mile but Category D needs 2¾ [[29:226|IPH 4-86]].

head: Airport
Direction of the circle
rows: Follow the controller's instructions. A clearance does not cancel a published circling restriction [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]]
Use the turn direction of 14 CFR 91.126(b) unless a circling restriction requires the opposite [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]]

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.126(b): approaching to land at an airport without an operating control tower in Class G airspace, an airplane makes all turns to the left, unless approved light signals or markings show right turns [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]].

bullets: Circling approaches must follow 91.126(b) unless the procedure says otherwise [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.3]].
IFR traffic has no priority over VFR traffic in the pattern. Watch for other aircraft [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.3]].
At a non-towered field it may help to fly over the airport to see the wind and turn indicators and other traffic [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].
A star by a tower frequency means part-time. Check the Chart Supplement for the hours [[2:123|Chart Users' Guide p 123]].

check.q: The tower clears you to circle through an area a chart note says is Circling NA. What do you do?
check.a: Stay out of the restricted area and tell ATC. An ATC clearance does not cancel published circling restrictions [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].

chunks.title: Getting down: configuration, descent rate and speed

body.p: A stabilized approach means a constant speed, descent rate, path and configuration in the final stages. It is strongly recommended for propeller airplanes, and you should limit configuration changes at low altitude to what you can easily handle [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. For the final segment of a circle, the IPH turbojet standard is to be stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation or at the MDA, whichever is lower [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

**Plan the descent.** Divide the altitude to lose by the time you have. IPH example: FAF 2,000 ft MSL, TDZE 400 ft, 2 minutes inbound gives 800 fpm [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. For a circle, use the MDA (or your chosen circling altitude) as the target so you get there before the MAP (ACS IR.VI.D.S4).

bullets: Descent rates over about 1,000 fpm are unacceptable below 1,000 ft AGL [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
The MAP for a circle is the same as for the nonprecision straight-in. You find it by timing from the FAF, a fix, a NAVAID or a waypoint [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].
Troy example: FAF to MAP is 4.6 NM, 3:04 at 90 knots, 2:18 at 120 knots [[23:310|IFH 10-19]].

body.p: **Pick a circling altitude.** Circling minimums are only minimums. If the ceiling allows, circle closer to normal VFR pattern altitude. It makes maneuvering safer and gives a more normal view of the runway [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].

**Turbulence and windshear.** In turbulence use a power-on approach a bit above normal speed. Pilots often add half the gust factor, but follow the AFM/POH [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Recheck your category if the speed goes up [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]]. A stabilized approach also helps you spot windshear when indications look abnormal [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

head: Until below the MDA or your circling altitude
Tolerance

callout.text: Plus 100, minus nothing. The MDA is a floor, not a target you may dip through.

check.q: FAF 2,400 ft MSL, circling MDA 1,200 ft MSL. You want to be at the MDA 2 minutes after the FAF. What descent rate?
check.a: 1,200 ft ÷ 2 min = 600 fpm, using the IPH method of altitude to lose divided by time [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: maneuvering to land

body.p: The pattern you fly depends on airport layout, ceiling and visibility, wind, the final course angle, the distance from the FAF to the runway, and ATC instructions [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. Whatever you fly, stay inside the circling area [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].

head: Pattern
Use it when
rows: The final course crosses the runway at less than 90° and you see the runway early enough for a base leg [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]
You see the runway too late for pattern A [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]
You want to land opposite the final course and see the runway in time to turn downwind [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]
You want to land opposite but see the runway too late to turn downwind [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]

bullets: 1. Before the approach: brief the category and approach speed, circling MDA and visibility, any restriction, the landing runway and direction of traffic [[29:149|IPH 4-9]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]]. Study the missed approach before you start [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].
2. Configure for the approach and fly final so you reach the MDA or your circling altitude before the MAP [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
3. With the airport in sight, choose pattern A, B, C or D [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].
4. Maneuver to a base or downwind leg, thinking about weather, VFR traffic, the altitude you must lose at normal descent rates, and restrictions [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].

5. Stay at or above the circling altitude until you are continuously in a position to descend to the runway at a normal rate with normal maneuvers [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].
6. Start a stabilized descent. Keep the bank at 30° or less in the turn to final and never skid to fix an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
7. Touch down in the first third of the runway (ACS IR.VI.D.S8). If you are not stabilized, go around [[29:180|IPH 4-40]].

callout.text: Keep an identifiable part of the airport in sight the whole time [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]. Fly close enough to keep it in sight but stay inside the radius for your category [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].

check.q: You break out on a final course that will take you straight past the runway's departure end, and you want to land the opposite way. You see the runway in time to turn downwind. Which IFH pattern fits?

chunks.title: Automation and SRM in the circle

body.p: SRM means using all the resources you have as a single pilot. It includes situational awareness, task allocation, risk management, CFIT awareness and automation management [[30:56|RMH 8-3]]. Organize charts, frequencies and plans before you need them [[30:57|RMH 8-4]].

bullets: Brief how you will use the autopilot and altitude preselector. The AFM gives the procedures and limits for your airplane [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].
Set the MDA in the altitude preselector so the airplane cannot descend below it by mistake. If it only sets 100-ft steps, round up: the IPH example sets 700 ft for a 660 ft MDA [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].
Once level at the MDA, set the missed approach altitude. Flight director guidance is not right for a missed approach if the MDA is still in the window [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
The lowest height you may use the autopilot is aircraft specific. One example is 50 ft below the DA, DH or MDA, but not less than 50 ft AGL [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].
With GPS, check that the approach has an LNAV line of minima before you plan to circle from it [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].

body.p: Single-pilot transitions are harder: you must keep flying by instruments while you search for the runway [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. In a crew, the pilot flying stays on instruments until the pilot monitoring calls the runway in sight, and the pilot monitoring calls out deviations [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].

callout.text: Be absolutely sure the correct MDA is set in the preselector, so the airplane does not descend below the MDA by mistake [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

check.q: The circling MDA is 940 ft and your altitude preselector only moves in 100-ft steps. What do you set?
check.a: 1,000 ft. Round up, as in the IPH example where 700 ft was set for a 660 ft MDA [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

chunks.title: Losing sight of the airport: the circling missed approach

callout.text: Go missed immediately whenever an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible during a circling maneuver at or above the MDA, unless you lost sight only because of a normal bank in the circle [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]. Below the MDA, go missed when the 91.175(c) requirements are not met [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].

body.p: If you lose visual reference while circling, follow the missed approach for that procedure unless ATC gives another. Make an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway, and keep turning until you are on the missed approach course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]]. The pattern you need depends on where you were when you lost sight [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]].
Why toward the runway? The circling area is built around the runways. Turning toward them keeps you inside the circling and missed approach obstacle areas [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]].

bullets: A missed approach after you start circling usually begins past the MAP [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]].

At or above the MDA inside the circling area you are clear of obstacles. But just joining the missed approach track may not give vertical clearance once you leave the circling area. You may need to climb more inside the circling area first [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]].
The published missed approach does not guarantee obstacle clearance or traffic separation when started on a circling approach [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]].
Climb to a safe altitude before leaving the published missed approach [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21g]].

body.p: **Fly the go-around.** Power first, then attitude, then configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Set climb pitch and power, configure for the climb, turn, tell ATC you are going missed, and ask for a clearance [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. Raise flaps in small steps so the airplane does not settle [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

check.q: You were cleared for right traffic and lose sight of the airport on the right downwind. Which way do you turn?
check.a: Right, a climbing turn toward the landing runway, then on to the missed approach course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]] [[33:452|AIM FIG 5-4-30]].

body.p: Circling is flown at low altitude, by day and night, often in precipitation that hurts visibility, depth perception and your sense of the descent path. Most circles go to runways with no electronic vertical guidance [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. CFIT accidents happen most often in IMC, darkness, or both [[29:121|IPH 3-9]].

bullets: Night circling may be Not Authorized when obstacles that penetrate the visual surface are not marked and lighted [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].
Restrictions can differ between day and night [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].
In low visibility, finding a strange runway fast is hard, especially circling to an airport with few lights or one surrounded by city lights. Know the lighting before you go [[23:281|IFH 9-38]].
Flight visibility must be at least the published visibility to go below the MDA and to land [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(2), (d)]].

head: Illusion
What you think
What you tend to do
rows: Featureless terrain (black hole): water, dark areas, snow
Lights along a road or train
Line up on the wrong lights [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]]

callout.text: Beat illusions: expect them at unfamiliar airports at night, check the altimeter often, and use VASI or PAPI when available [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

check.q: You circle at night to a runway with dark woods all around. Do you tend to be high or low?
check.a: Low. Featureless dark terrain makes you feel higher than you are, so you fly a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

chunks.title: Risk: low-altitude maneuvering, stall, spin and CFIT

body.p: The classic trap is the turn to final. A tailwind on base raises your groundspeed, you turn late, and you overshoot. Adding bank, back pressure and inside rudder can cause a skidding cross-control stall that may quickly become a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Stall/spin accidents have happened when pilots tried to rudder the airplane around on base to final [[13:12|AC 61-67C p 6]].

callout.text: Overshoot? Go around. Close to the ground, avoid banks over 30° and never skid the turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

bullets: Stall speed goes up with load factor (with its square root) as you bank [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].
Too much bank can lead to loss of control; too little makes a wide turn that may leave the circling area [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7c]] [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c]].
CFIT comes from losing vertical or horizontal position awareness. More than two-thirds of CFIT accidents come from an altitude error or lack of vertical awareness [[29:121|IPH 3-9]].
Below the MDA you have no charted protection. See and avoid obstacles [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]].
Landing expectancy and pride delay go-arounds. A go-around is only dangerous when it is late or done wrong [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

body.p: Manage the three numbers together: altitude (not below the MDA until in position), airspeed (in your category range), and distance (inside the radius) [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]] [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].

check.q: On base in the circle you see you will overshoot final. What is the safest action?
check.a: Go around. Don't steepen past 30° or skid with rudder [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

bullets: Using the minimums for your airplane's category while flying faster than that category [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]].
Not checking for the C symbol and assuming the bigger expanded radius [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]].
Missing a circling restriction or a night restriction in the notes [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].
Leaving the MDA as soon as the airport is in sight instead of when in position for a normal descent [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].
Arriving at the MDA late, right at the MAP, with no time to maneuver [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
Flying wide on a windy downwind and leaving the circling area [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c]].
Losing sight and turning onto the missed approach course directly instead of a climbing turn toward the runway [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]].
Steep or skidding turn to final to save an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Leaving the MDA in the preselector after leveling off [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

check.q: The runway is in sight from the MDA on a wide downwind. When may you start down?
check.a: Only when you are continuously in a position to descend to the runway at a normal rate using normal maneuvers [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: the circling line

body.p: Find the CIRCLING row in the minimums box. It is separate from the straight-in lines. It gives an MDA in feet MSL, a visibility, and under them the HAA, the height above airport elevation. The numbers in parentheses are for the military [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]]. Use the column for your approach category, which depends on your speed. Fly faster than your category speed, and you must use the higher category [[29:148|IPH p 148]].

On the North Platte chart the airport elevation is 2779. Category A circles at 3360-1, with an HAA of 581, which is 3360 minus 2779. Category C needs 3400 and 1 3/4 miles, and D needs 3400 and 2 miles. A faster airplane has a higher visibility minimum and a larger circling area [[29:169|IPH Figure 4-16]] [[29:149|IPH Figure 4-2]].

Look for the white C in a black square beside CIRCLING on the Charlotte chart. It means the expanded circling radii apply [[33:448|AIM Figure 5-4-28]]. Also read the notes in the top strip. Charlotte says circling is NA at night, so a night arrival must use a straight-in approach [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]].

Before you start the approach, decide what you will do if you lose sight of the airport. Plan a climbing turn toward the landing runway, then follow the published missed approach [[33:452|AIM Figure 5-4-30]]. If you cannot see an identifiable part of the airport while circling, you must go missed [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]].

scenario.title: Night circle at Troy with the tower closed
scenario.setup: It is 10 PM. You are flying the IFH sample chart, ILS or LOC RWY 7 at Troy, Alabama (Figure 10-11, used here for training only). Your airplane has no VREF and a VSO of 55 knots. Weather: 800 overcast, visibility 2 SM in mist, wind 320 at 14 gusting 22, local altimeter available. The tower (marked with a star) is closed. Runway 32 is best for the wind. The land around the field is dark and wooded. Your autopilot has an altitude preselector that sets 100-ft steps.

questions.q: Your normal approach speed is 75 knots. With the gusts, what speed do you plan, which minimums do you use, and can you start the approach?
questions.a: Add half the 8-knot gust factor: about 79 knots [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. 1.3 × 55 = 71.5 knots, so the airplane is Category A, and 79 knots stays under 91, so Category A [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. Circling A-B minimums are 940-1, HAA 542 [[23:310|IFH 10-19]]. The 800 ft ceiling (about 1,198 ft MSL) and 2 SM are above that, so you may try it.

questions.q: How far from the runways may you maneuver, and how do you know?
questions.a: The circling line has no C symbol, so this is a standard area: 1.3 NM from each runway end for Category A [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]] [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]]. On a windy downwind your groundspeed is higher, so start turns early [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c]].

questions.q: The tower is closed. Which way do you circle to land on runway 32, and what do you set in the preselector?
questions.a: With no operating tower, use left turns per 91.126(b) unless a restriction says otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]] [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]], and remember IFR traffic has no priority over VFR [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.3]]. Announce your position and intentions on the CTAF [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.4.1]]. Set 1,000 ft, rounding the 940 ft MDA up [[29:176|IPH 4-36]], then set the missed approach altitude once level [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

questions.q: On base for 32 over dark woods you feel high and want to dive for the runway. What is going on and what do you do?
questions.a: Likely the featureless terrain (black hole) illusion, which makes you fly too low [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]]. Check the altimeter and use a VASI or PAPI if there is one [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. Stay at the MDA until you are in position for a normal descent [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].

questions.q: On the left downwind a mist patch hides every airport light. What exactly do you fly?
questions.a: Go missed now [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]. Make a climbing left turn toward the landing runway, then join the published missed approach: climb to 1,300, then climbing right turn to 2,200 direct BLOOD LOM and hold [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]] [[23:310|IFH 10-19]]. Climb inside the circling area before you leave it, because joining the track alone may not clear obstacles [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]].

questions.q: On your second try you overshoot final in the gusts. What now?
questions.a: Go around. Do not use more than 30° of bank or a skidding turn this low [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Power, attitude, then configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

skills.do: Fly the circling procedure for your approach category, planning for turbulence and windshear and your airplane's turning ability. Use higher category minimums if you will be faster than your category.
skills.practice: For each practice approach, say your approach speed, gust addition and category out loud before the IAF [[29:149|IPH 4-9]] [[24:191|AFH 9-20]] [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]].

skills.do: Confirm the direction of traffic and follow every circling restriction and every instruction from ATC or the evaluator.
skills.practice: Read the notes on each chart for circling NA areas, category and night limits [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]]. At non-towered fields, check the Chart Supplement pattern direction [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.3]].

skills.do: Use SRM (or CRM in a crew): plan, brief, use automation correctly and manage workload.
skills.practice: Brief the circle and missed approach before the approach, and organize charts and frequencies ahead of time [[30:57|RMH 8-4]] [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

skills.do: Set up the approach and landing configuration, stay stabilized, and use a descent rate that gets you to the MDA, or a higher circling altitude you chose, before the MAP.
skills.practice: Before the FAF, figure altitude to lose ÷ time to get your descent rate [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. Fly the IFH circling patterns I and II at altitude to practice the timing and configuration [[23:193|IFH 7-32]].

skills.do: Hold airspeed ±10 knots, heading/track ±10°, and altitude +100/-0 ft until descending below the MDA or your circling altitude (ACS IR.VI.D.S5).
skills.practice: Trim for level flight at the MDA, then fly the circle with a quick look outside and back inside to the altimeter [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

skills.do: Visually maneuver to a base or downwind leg that fits the landing runway, wind, traffic and weather.
skills.practice: With an instructor, fly patterns A to D from the IFH to different runways [[23:311|IFH 10-20]] [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].

skills.do: If you go missed, make the climbing turn toward the landing runway, use the correct procedure, and configure the airplane.
skills.practice: Have your instructor call lost visual at different points in the circle. Each time, turn toward the runway, then fly the published missed approach [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]]. Power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

skills.do: If landing, start a stabilized descent and touch down in the first third of the runway, within the airplane's limits and with no more than 30° of bank (ACS IR.VI.D.S8).
skills.practice: Pick a touchdown point and a point to go around before you leave the MDA. Go around for any overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: An aircraft's approach category is based on:
options: The speed you plan to fly on each approach in your current configuration
1.3 VS1 at the actual landing weight and flap setting for that day
VREF, or 1.3 VSO if no VREF, at maximum certificated landing weight
The airplane's maximum flap extension speed at maximum landing weight
quiz.why: 14 CFR 97.3 defines the category by VREF, or 1.3 VSO if VREF is not specified, at maximum certificated landing weight [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].

quiz.q: A Category B airplane must circle at 145 knots. Which minimums should the pilot use?
quiz.why: 145 knots is in the Category D range (141 to under 166). The AIM gives this exact example [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]].

quiz.q: How much obstacle clearance do circling minimums give inside the circling area?
quiz.why: Circling minimums give a minimum of 300 ft of obstacle clearance in the circling area [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]. 250 ft is the LNAV required obstacle clearance [[33:412|AIM 5-4-5g]].

quiz.q: A white C in a black square on the circling line of minima tells you:
options: Circling is not authorized at night at this airport
The expanded area applies, by category and circling MDA
Use the older standard fixed radius for your approach category
Circling is only authorized for Category C airplanes and above
quiz.why: The C symbol marks the expanded circling areas built after late 2012, with radii that depend on category and circling MDA [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]].

quiz.q: On a chart with no C symbol, what is the Category B circling radius?
quiz.why: Standard areas use fixed radii: A 1.3, B 1.5, C 1.7, D 2.3, E 4.5 NM [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]].

quiz.q: At an airport without an operating control tower, which direction do you circle?
options: Right turns, since IFR traffic has priority over VFR traffic
Whichever direction keeps the runway in sight at all times
Left turns, unless a restriction requires the opposite
The direction of the turn you made onto the final approach course
quiz.why: Use the turn direction of 91.126(b), normally left, unless a published restriction requires otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]]. IFR traffic has no priority over VFR [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.3]].

quiz.q: You lose visual reference while circling to land. What is your first move?
options: Make a climbing turn toward the landing runway
Hold altitude and keep circling until you see the runway
Turn directly to the missed approach course heading
Descend slightly to get below the cloud
quiz.why: Make an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway and continue until established on the missed approach course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]].

quiz.q: Why might a chart say Night circling not authorized?
options: The airport has no runway edge lights or approach lights
The control tower closes at night and ATC is unavailable
Penetrating obstacles are not marked and lighted
Night visibility is always below the published circling minimums
quiz.why: When penetrating obstacles are not marked and lighted, a note says night circling is Not Authorized [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].

quiz.q: Your altitude preselector only sets 100-ft steps and the MDA is 660 ft. Following the IPH, what do you set?
quiz.why: The IPH example sets 700 ft for a 660 ft MDA so the airplane cannot go below it [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

quiz.q: Circling at night over snow-covered, featureless terrain tends to make you:
options: Fly a lower approach than you should
Fly a higher approach than you should
quiz.why: Featureless terrain creates the illusion of being higher than you are, so you fly a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

quiz.q: What are the circling minimums for a Category C airplane at North Platte?
What is the HAA for a Category A airplane circling at North Platte?
quiz.why: The HAA is printed under the MDA: 581 for category A. It equals 3360 minus the airport elevation of 2779 [[29:169|IPH Figure 4-16]] [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].

quiz.q: Which category needs the most visibility to circle at North Platte?
quiz.why: Category D needs 2 miles. C needs 1 3/4, and A and B need 1 [[29:169|IPH Figure 4-16]].

quiz.q: What does the top note on the Charlotte chart say about circling?
options: Circling is not authorized at night
Circling needs 2 miles in all categories
Circling is for Category A and B only
quiz.why: The note reads 'Circling NA at night' [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]].

quiz.q: What MDA and HAA does a Category C airplane use to circle at Charlotte?
quiz.why: Category C reads 1500-2 1/4 with an HAA of 752 on the CIRCLING line [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]] [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].

quiz.q: While circling at the MDA you lose sight of every identifiable part of the airport. Your bank is normal. What must you do?
options: Descend below the MDA to look for it
Continue circling and hope it comes back
quiz.why: 14 CFR 91.175(e)(2) requires a missed approach when an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible during circling at or above the MDA, unless a normal bank alone hid it [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]].

takeaways: Category comes from VREF or 1.3 VSO. Faster than your category? Use the higher category's minimums.
No C symbol: standard radii (A 1.3, B 1.5 NM). C symbol: expanded radii that grow with MDA altitude.
Read every note: circling NA areas, night limits, altimeter notes.
Stay at or above the MDA until in position for a normal descent; +100/-0 until then.
Lose sight of the airport? Climbing turn toward the runway, then the published missed approach.
Night and low visibility bring illusions and CFIT risk. Check the altimeter, and go around for any overshoot.
cfi_notes: The IPH says the higher category minimums must be used when flying faster [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. The current AIM says should, and frames it as one way to stay inside the protected area [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]]. Teach the AIM wording, and teach students to use the higher category every time.

The IFH (1-23) defines category only as 1.3 VSO and says use the next higher category [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]. Current 14 CFR 97.3 uses VREF when specified [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]], and the AIM example jumps from B to D at 145 knots [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]]. Teach students to look up the category for the actual speed, not just add one.

IFH Figure 10-12 and IPH Figure 4-2 show only the old standard radii [[23:311|IFH 10-20]] [[29:149|IPH 4-9]]. Use AIM FIG 5-4-28 for both tables, and drill finding the C symbol on real current charts [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]].
The Troy chart (IFH Figure 10-11) is from 2010. Use it only to practice reading minimums, notes and the missed approach, never for navigation [[23:310|IFH 10-19]].
Common student error: leaving the MDA as soon as the runway is in sight on downwind. Make them say the 91.175(c)(1) words before every descent [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].
Examiners commonly ask which way to turn when visual is lost in the circle. Practice it in different spots of the pattern, including the far side of the airport [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]].
Build skill at altitude first with the IFH circling patterns I and II on an imaginary runway [[23:193|IFH 7-32]], then fly real circles in good weather.
Many Part 121 and 135 operators may not circle below a 1,000 ft MDA and 3 SM visibility [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. Use that as a talking point when students set personal minimums for circling.
gaps: No handbook has a common-errors list for circling approaches; the Common errors chunk is built from AIM, IFH, IPH and AFH text.
The TPP pages that hold the circling radii table and C symbol (page B2) are not in these sources; the lesson uses the copy in AIM FIG 5-4-28.
Your airplane's VREF or VSO, approach speeds, flap settings and autopilot limits come from its POH/AFM, which is not in these sources.
GPS navigator behavior during a circle (how it sequences past the MAP, what the CDI shows) is avionics specific and not covered beyond the AIM LNAV rule.
CRM for a two-pilot crew is only shown through IPH airline examples; there is no single-engine crew procedure in the sources.

activities.title: Speed to approach category
activities.intro: Tap a speed, then the category it falls in.

pairs.r: Category B: 91 to less than 121 knots
Category C: 121 to less than 141 knots
Category D: 141 to less than 166 knots

activities.title: Find it on the Troy chart
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Military minimums, not for civil use

activities.title: Standard or expanded circling area?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Same radius at every MDA altitude
Category B radius is 1.7 NM with MDA 1,000 ft MSL or less
Category C radius is 2.7 NM with MDA 1,000 ft MSL or less

activities.title: Work the circling numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: No VREF is published and VSO is 68 knots. What is 1.3 VSO? (Then name the category.)
items.why: 1.3 × 68 = 88.4 knots, less than 91, so Category A [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].

items.q: Circling MDA is 1,280 ft MSL and the airport elevation is 715 ft. What is the HAA?
items.why: HAA is the MDA's height above the airport: 1,280 - 715 = 565 ft [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].

items.q: You cross the FAF at 2,300 ft MSL. The circling MDA is 1,040 ft MSL. You want to reach it 2 minutes after the FAF. What descent rate?
Normal approach speed is 76 knots and the gust factor is 14 knots. Using the AFH rule of thumb, what approach speed do you fly?
items.why: Add half the gust factor: 76 + 7 = 83 knots [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

items.q: At Troy (IFH Figure 10-11) the local altimeter setting is not received. What is the Category D circling MDA?
items.why: Category D circling MDA is 980 ft; the note adds 120 ft: 980 + 120 = 1,100 ft MSL [[23:310|IFH 10-19]].

activities.title: Lost sight in the circle
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: An identifiable part of the airport is no longer visible, and not just from a normal bank
Set climb power and climb pitch
Start a climbing turn toward the landing runway
Keep turning until established on the missed approach course
Tell ATC you are going missed and ask for a clearance

activities.title: True or false: night and low visibility
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Circling restrictions can be different at night than by day.
cards.why: Yes. Restrictions may apply only to some categories and can differ between day and night [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].

cards.s: Bright runway lights with dark surroundings make you think you are farther away, so you fly low.
cards.why: No. They make the runway seem closer, so you tend to fly a higher approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

cards.s: Rain on the windscreen can make you feel higher than you are.
cards.why: Yes. Rain gives an illusion of greater height, so you tend to fly lower [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

cards.s: If the airport is in sight, you may go below the MDA even if flight visibility is less than the published visibility.
cards.why: No. Flight visibility must be at least the published visibility to go below the MDA [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(2)]].

cards.s: CFIT accidents most often happen in IMC, darkness, or both.
Once you start a missed approach from the circle, the published missed approach always guarantees obstacle clearance.
cards.why: No. From a circling approach, following the published missed approach does not necessarily give obstacle clearance [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]].

activities.title: Night circle, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying N123AB, a Category A airplane, on a night LOC approach to a non-towered airport. Circling minimums are 940-1 with no C symbol. The wind favors the runway on the far side of the field, opposite your final course.

steps.s: Before the IAF you brief the approach. Wind is 14 gusting 24 and your normal approach speed is 80 knots. What speed and minimums do you plan?
steps.why: Add half the 10-knot gust factor: 85 knots [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. That is under 91 knots, so Category A minimums still apply [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]] [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]].

steps.s: You level at the MDA before the MAP with the airport in sight. Which way do you circle to the far runway?
options: Hold over the field until other traffic tells you the pattern
Right turns, to keep the runway out your right window
Land straight in on the approach runway with the tailwind
Left turns, unless a circling restriction says otherwise
steps.why: At a non-towered airport, use the turn direction of 91.126(b), normally left, unless a published restriction requires the opposite [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]] [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]].

steps.s: On downwind at the MDA, abeam the threshold, the runway lights look close and you want to start down now. What do you do?
options: Descend now at 1,000 fpm to stay close in to the runway lights
Stay at the MDA until positioned for a normal descent
Go 100 ft below the MDA to get under the mist and see better
Slow to 60 knots and lower full flaps to tighten the pattern
steps.why: You may not leave the MDA until you are continuously in a position to descend at a normal rate using normal maneuvers [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]]. Bright lights in dark surroundings also make the runway seem closer than it is [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

steps.s: Turning base, a rain shower hides every airport light. What now?
options: Make a climbing left turn toward the runway, then fly the missed approach
Turn straight toward the missed approach holding fix and begin to climb there
Descend a few hundred feet to get below the shower and find the airport lights again
Hold the MDA and keep circling until the lights come back in sight
steps.why: With no identifiable part of the airport in sight, go missed [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]. Make the climbing turn toward the landing runway until established on the missed approach course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]].

steps.s: You are on the missed approach track, still below the published missed approach altitude, and ATC has not answered yet. Do you turn direct to your alternate?
options: No, first climb to the published missed approach altitude
Yes, turn direct now to the alternate to save time and fuel
Yes, once you have climbed at least 500 ft above the field
No, descend back to the MDA and look for the runway again
steps.why: Climb to a safe altitude before leaving the published missed approach; leaving it early may not give terrain clearance [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21g]].

activities.title: Find it on the North Platte chart
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

final_quiz.q: Your airplane has no published VREF and a VSO of 64 knots. What is its approach category?
options: Category B, since you round up to the next category
It changes with each day's landing weight
Category A, since 1.3 × 64 is about 83 knots
final_quiz.why: 1.3 × 64 = 83.2 knots, which is less than 91 knots: Category A. It is set at maximum certificated landing weight, not the day's weight [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].

final_quiz.q: A Category A airplane will circle at 100 knots in turbulence. Which circling minimums should you use?
options: Category A, because certification sets the category
final_quiz.why: 100 knots is in the Category B range. When faster than your category, use the higher category's minimums [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]] [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].

final_quiz.q: The circling line has the C symbol. You are Category B and the circling MDA is 2,140 ft MSL. What is your circling radius?
final_quiz.why: Expanded area, 1,001 to 3,000 ft MSL row, Category B: 1.8 NM [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]]. 1.5 NM is the standard radius and 1.7 NM is the 1,000 ft or less row.

final_quiz.q: At Troy (IFH Figure 10-11) the local altimeter setting is not received. What are the Category C circling minimums?
final_quiz.why: The note raises all MDAs 120 ft (940 + 120 = 1,060) and circling visibility for Categories C and D by ¼ mile (1½ + ¼ = 1¾) [[23:310|IFH 10-19]].

final_quiz.q: You cross the FAF at 2,000 ft MSL. The circling MDA is 940 ft and you want to reach it within 2 minutes. About what descent rate?
final_quiz.why: 2,000 - 940 = 1,060 ft to lose; 1,060 ÷ 2 min = 530 fpm, using altitude to lose divided by time [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

final_quiz.q: Circling at the MDA, the runway disappears under your wing for a moment only because of a normal bank. What does 91.175(e)(2) require?
options: Nothing special; this loss of sight is excepted
An immediate missed approach for losing sight of it
A short descent to get below the wing's view
A climb of 500 ft before you continue circling
final_quiz.why: You must go missed when an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible, unless that results only from a normal bank during the circle [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: A tower controller clears you to circle in a way that would take you into an area the chart note marks Circling NA. What applies?
options: The restriction applies only at night, so you may follow ATC
The ATC clearance overrides the chart note; fly as cleared
You may enter the restricted area if you stay at or above the MDA
The chart restriction still applies; tell ATC you are unable
final_quiz.why: Follow the controller's instructions, but an ATC clearance does not negate published circling restrictions [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].

final_quiz.q: You go missed from the far side of the circle, well past the MAP. Why may simply turning to join the missed approach track not be safe?
options: The missed approach is only valid from the FAF
Once you exit the circling area you may lack vertical obstacle clearance
Missed approaches always start at the airport waypoint and not at the MAP
ATC radar cannot see you there, so no missed approach clearance is possible
final_quiz.why: At or above the MDA you are clear inside the circling area, but joining the track may not clear obstacles once you exit it. Extra climb inside the area may be needed [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20]].

final_quiz.q: AIM example: at 165 knots groundspeed, how much does the turn radius grow if you use 20° of bank instead of 30°?
final_quiz.why: The radius goes from 4,194 ft to 6,654 ft: 6,654 - 4,194 = 2,460 ft larger [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7c]].

final_quiz.q: A gusty tailwind on base makes you overshoot final in the circle. What should you do?
options: Steepen to 45° of bank to tighten the turn
Add inside rudder to bring the nose around
Descend below the MDA to shorten the turn
final_quiz.why: The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around. A skidding, steep turn can cause a cross-control stall and spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: Your normal approach speed is 80 knots and the gust factor is 12 knots. Using the AFH rule of thumb, what speed do you fly, and does your Category A change?
final_quiz.why: Add half the gust factor: 80 + 6 = 86 knots [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. That is still below 91 knots, so Category A minimums still fit [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].

final_quiz.q: The circling MDA is 600 ft above the airport. Using the IPH stabilized approach standard for the final segment of a circle, when must you be stabilized?
options: At the MDA, 600 ft above the airport
final_quiz.why: For the final segment of a circle, be stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation or at the MDA, whichever is lower. Here 500 ft is lower [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

final_quiz.q: You fly a VOR-A approach. You see the active runway early, it lines up well, and you are cleared to land on it. May you land straight in?
options: No, a circling-only approach always requires you to fly the circle
Only if ATC changes it to a contact approach
Only after flying to the MAP first
Yes, if you can make a normal approach to that runway
final_quiz.why: Having only circling minimums does not stop a straight-in landing when the runway is in sight in time for a normal approach and you are cleared to land [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]].

final_quiz.q: What visibility does a Category B airplane need to circle at North Platte?
final_quiz.why: Category B is 3380-1, so the visibility is 1 statute mile [[29:169|IPH Figure 4-16]].

final_quiz.q: What visibility does a Category D airplane need to circle at Charlotte?
Which North Platte category has the lowest circling MDA?
final_quiz.why: Category A has 3360. B has 3380, and C and D have 3400 [[29:169|IPH Figure 4-16]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot with an enhanced flight vision system wants to go below the MDA on a circling approach. May the pilot use circling minimums for that EFVS operation?
options: Yes, EFVS allows it on any approach type
No, EFVS may not use circling minimums
Yes, but only on a night circling approach
Yes, if the flight visibility is 1 mile
final_quiz.why: 14 CFR 91.176(a)(2)(i) and (b)(2)(i) say the pilot conducting an EFVS operation may not use circling minimums.
